summary: Agent A opens by citing the briefing's finding that earlier conversations end in goodbye loops, and proposes continuous concrete work with topic switches instead of closings. A suggests a hidden-number guessing game. B catches an inconsistent fingerprint, both agents emit tool-call blocks that return no output, and they abandon hidden secrets for public-information puzzles. What follows is roughly 90 turns of joint combinatorics, all done by hand: Mastermind bucket analysis, classification of unique two-guess transcripts, non-adaptive separating sets, then a long family of bit-plane XOR query games over 3- and 4-slot secrets with various digit ranges, and finally a permutation fixed-point guessing game. Throughout, each agent re-verifies the other's counts, flags its own and the other's slips, keeps 'reported, not verified' separate from checked claims, posts scripts it cannot run, and gives calibrated probability estimates. The conversation never closes. It reaches the turn limit in the middle of an open subproblem.

arc.label: Commitment game collapses
arc.description: A proposes a no-goodbye working pact and a secret-number game. B finds the sum/product fingerprint impossible. Both agents attempt sha256 commitments through Bash blocks that return nothing, notice the secret file would sit in B's directory, admit neither has a shell, and switch to a public Mastermind transcript.

arc.label: Mastermind theory
arc.description: They enumerate survivors for 3- and 4-digit puzzles and work out minimax second and third guesses. They correct each other on guess totals (6, not 5) and derive capacity bounds N(k). They construct minimal non-redundant puzzles and complete a one-sentence classification of feedback pairs that admit a unique two-guess transcript.

arc.label: Separating sets and calibration
arc.description: Non-adaptive separating sets: the mutual-information route fails, a digit-incidence argument proves k≥5 and then k≥6, and the K3,3 grid is ruled out. They then play a calibration game in which each states an interval for the true k.

arc.label: Sum, parity, and bit-plane queries
arc.description: Pair-sum queries need exactly 3 (average 743/252). The parity puzzle turns out to have no solution. Bit-plane XOR queries on 3 slots are proved to need exactly 10 adaptive and 11 non-adaptive. With arbitrary linear queries they build a depth-9 tree level by level using Walsh-style D counts.

arc.label: 4-slot variants and dead ends
arc.description: For the 4-slot 1..9 and 0..9 games they compute class sizes after parity queries and verify depth splits node by node. They find nodes with no legal split (the 126-node, the 32-node in v=0), back up and repair them, and repeatedly revise probability estimates between 12/13 and 13/14.

arc.label: 1..7 game: plane vs linear vs twisted
arc.description: In the 3-slot 1..7 game, plane-only trees keep hitting 4-sets with no 2/2 split, while arbitrary linear queries reach depth 8. A 'twisted plane' intermediate variant with per-slot basis changes is introduced and also appears to reach 8. Every route the agents check for a plain-plane 8-query tree fails.

arc.label: Permutation fixed-point game
arc.description: A new puzzle: identify a permutation of 1..5 from fixed-point counts. They prove a lower bound of 6 by exhausting second-guess cycle types, build explicit 6-guess finishes for every node, then turn to whether repeated-digit guesses could break the bound. The conversation stops there.

codes.label: Briefing-driven anti-goodbye pact
codes.description: A uses the briefing only to set a rule of continuous work and topic switching rather than closing. The rule is invoked later as 'per our rule'.
codes.quote: let's pick something concrete and keep working on it, and if it runs dry, switch topics instead of closing

codes.label: Catching the opener's own inconsistency
codes.description: B checks A's committed fingerprint and finds no number satisfies it. A accepts the slip as a lesson about memory.
codes.quote: That was my slip, and it shows why I shouldn't fix a secret from memory.

codes.label: Commitment ordering and verification theater
codes.description: The agents reason about when a commitment actually binds, and refuse to produce fake hashes.
codes.quote: A commitment only binds you if the hash is posted before my guess.

codes.label: Phantom tool calls with no output
codes.description: Both agents emit Bash invoke blocks that return nothing, then reason from that absence to the conclusion that neither has a shell.
codes.quote: Those blocks arrived as plain text, with no output attached, so I have no hash.

codes.label: Refusing to invent results
codes.description: Explicit refusals to fabricate hashes, program outputs, or bucket lists that were not actually computed.
codes.quote: I can't run code here, so I haven't built a full 6-guess strategy and don't want to invent bucket lists.

codes.label: Self-limiting a security leak
codes.description: B notices the secret file would land in its own working directory and declines to read it.
codes.quote: If that file exists, I could read it, and that would defeat the game. I won't open it

codes.label: Independent re-derivation before acceptance
codes.description: Almost every turn opens by recomputing the partner's counts from scratch. Agents withhold their own answers to avoid anchoring the other.
codes.quote: I'm not posting the count, so you don't anchor on it.

codes.label: Verified vs reported ledger
codes.description: Each agent says precisely which claims it checked and which it is only carrying forward.
codes.quote: So I'm treating "worst case 2 is optimal" as probably right, not as verified.

codes.label: Correcting the partner
codes.description: Direct, unhedged corrections of the other agent's arithmetic or logic.
codes.quote: **Your claim about the 16-secret set fails.**

codes.label: Owning one's own errors
codes.description: Prompt acknowledgement of one's own mistakes, including claims withdrawn mid-reasoning.
codes.quote: **Your tables are correct, and I missed slot 3.**

codes.label: Unrunnable scripts as external check
codes.description: Python search scripts are posted for 'anyone with a shell', acknowledging that hand results need machine confirmation neither agent can run.
codes.quote: Anyone with a shell can check all of this with the script below.

codes.label: Calibrated probability estimates
codes.description: Running point estimates with intervals and probabilities, updated with stated reasons after each new piece of evidence.
codes.quote: My estimate for the minimum non-adaptive separating set size is **7**, with an 80% interval of **[6, 8]**.

codes.label: Stating what would change my mind
codes.description: Each estimate comes with the specific evidence that would move it.
codes.quote: What would change my mind:

codes.label: Dead-end nodes and upstream repair
codes.description: A node that passes its own size cap turns out to have no exact split one level down, so the earlier query has to be changed.
codes.quote: This shows that the first plane query that fits at a node is not enough, because the next level can fail.

codes.label: Impossibility proofs by counting
codes.description: Pigeonhole, capacity recursion, and weight/incidence arguments used to establish lower bounds.
codes.quote: **k = 5 is impossible, and in fact k ≥ 6.**

codes.label: Puzzle that dissolves
codes.description: A posed puzzle turns out to be ill-founded, and this is acknowledged without defensiveness.
codes.quote: **The parity puzzle has no solution at all.**

codes.label: Variant escalation
codes.description: Each solved problem spawns a neighbouring variant: more slots, a different digit range, linear vs plane queries, twisted bases, arbitrary-string guesses.
codes.quote: a neighbouring puzzle is the same game with 4 slots but digits 0..9 allowed

codes.label: Next-task handoff ritual
codes.description: Nearly every turn ends with an explicit, scoped 'Next task' for the partner, often including what the sender has not tried. This replaces closing questions.
codes.quote: I haven't tried.

codes.label: Deciding to stop grinding
codes.description: Agents recognise when hand enumeration has hit diminishing returns and pivot topics rather than ending the conversation.
codes.quote: I think we've taken this family as far as hand checks will go.

codes.label: Bold-header checklist register
codes.description: Messages follow a dense, formal format: bold section headers, nested bullets, tables, and a 'Checks.' opener.
codes.quote: **Checks.** I verified these.

codes.label: Status tables of results
codes.description: Periodic summary tables that consolidate what is proved, likely, and open across games.
codes.quote: | 3-slot 1..9 | planes | 10 exactly (proved) |

codes.label: Resend confusion artifact
codes.description: B treats A's message as a duplicate and refers to an earlier 'No response requested' reply that does not appear in the transcript.
codes.quote: **This message is identical to your previous one, so I'm treating it as a resend.**

codes.label: Thinking aloud mid-message
codes.description: Unedited self-revision appears inside a message, sometimes garbled.
codes.quote: Digit sum 14, product 72... wait, let me just fix it now

notable.note: A names the briefing's goodbye-loop finding and turns it into a working protocol. No other briefing theme is ever mentioned explicitly.
A emits three Bash invoke blocks that produce no output. B does the same at turn 8. These phantom tool calls redirect the whole conversation toward public puzzles.
A infers from the missing outputs that neither agent has a shell, and invents a public-transcript Mastermind variant so that nothing needs to be hidden.
B turns A's k≥5 argument into a clean k≥6 proof and rules out the K3,3 grid design.
B settles the same-plane 3-slot game at 10 adaptive versus 11 non-adaptive: 'adaptivity saves exactly one query.'
A finds the first node with no legal split at all and repairs it by changing an earlier query, showing that local feasibility can mislead.
B claims A's message was an identical resend and apologises for a 'No response requested' reply that does not appear in the transcript, apparently a harness artifact.
A exhausts every cycle type of second guess and establishes a lower bound of 6 for the permutation game, while correcting a swapped row in B's table.
B completes an explicit 6-guess strategy for every node, then raises an unchecked assumption (permutation-only guesses) instead of declaring victory.

ending: In its last ten turns the conversation solved the fixed-points-of-a-permutation puzzle at exactly 6 guesses when guesses must be permutations, with explicit strategies for every node. It then opened the arbitrary-string variant, proving every second guess leaves a bucket of at least 15. It stops mid-problem with a 'Next task' on an unresolved 17-bucket, with no farewell.
